summary: Not unrenderable at all: this is a var-driven mapper helper, and once the exported variable is written both sides light exactly one pure-red pixel at the requested index, byte-identical across every value, rig, pixel count, seed, clock and window — but the port renames the exported var (orig 'pixel' vs port 'pixelIndex') so no client written for the original can drive it, and when undriven (or given any negative index) the port runs a self-scanning demo that the original, confirmed via --no-vars, does not have.
observations: SUPERSEDES the previous orig-unrenderable/score-0 verdict. That verdict was correct only for an undriven run: with the fixup manifest's vars pin applied (meta.json provenance.fixups.vars = {orig:{pixel:30}, port:{pixelIndex:30}}), BOTH sides render. The original is not broken.
Control surface: both sides expose ZERO settable controls (--probe-controls printed '(no settable controls)' for orig and port). The entire input surface is the exported var.

VAR NAME DIVERGENCE (the headline port finding): meta.json sides.orig.varsExported = ["pixel"], sides.port.varsExported = ["pixelIndex"]. Same semantics, different name. A Pixelblaze mapper/companion client that writes 'pixel' would leave the port entirely undriven (and therefore in its auto-scan state, see below).

Driven behaviour, default rig (strip, 60 px, 20 fps): with the var set to N, both sides light exactly ONE pixel — index N, colour exactly (255,0,0) — and nothing else. All other 59 pixels are exactly (0,0,0). Verified byte-identical at N = 0, 1, 7, 29, 30, 31, 44, 59.

Both sides are STATIC when driven: motion avg/min/max = 0, motionLit = 0, zeroMotionFrames = 120/120 over the 6 s baseline and 300/300 over the 60 s / 5 fps survey; brightnessTrend 'steady' on both; meanR pinned at 4, meanG = meanB = 0 on both. The waterfalls are a single 1-px red vertical line at column 30 on both sides, indistinguishable.
Steady state confirmed: --skip 120 --seconds 6 dumps at t=120.0 s and t=125.9 s are still byte-identical single red pixel at index 30 on both sides. No decay, no drift, no late divergence.
Seed and wall clock are irrelevant and agree: --seed 1234 and --wall-clock 1700003600 both give byte-identical orig/port frames at t=0 and t=1.9 s (still pixel 30 red).

Index selection is strict equality on the integer pixel index, identically on both sides: fractional values 0.5, 29.7 and 30.5 render FULLY BLACK (0 lit pixels) on orig AND port — neither side rounds or floors. Out-of-range positives 60, 61 and 100 on a 60-px strip also render fully black on both sides.

Geometry independence, both sides byte-identical: --pixels 12 with value 5 lights index 5; --pixels 300 with value 201 lights index 201; a full 300-px sweep at values 5, 59, 60, 64, 100, 127, 128, 150, 200, 255, 299 lights exactly that index on both sides every time (no 8-bit or fixed-point index ceiling on either side); --rig grid --grid 32x8 with value 100 lights flat index 100 (row 3, col 4) on both; --rig cloud --pixels 125 with value 77 lights index 77 on both. The pattern is pure flat-index addressing on both sides, with no rig dependence.

OUT-OF-BAND / UNDRIVEN DIVERGENCE: at a negative index the two sides part company. orig at pixel=-1: meanBrightness 0 on every frame, motion 0, ZERO lit pixels at t = 0, 0.05, 0.1, 0.15, 0.2, 0.25, 0.5, 1, 2, 3, 5, 7.9 s, and mean 0 across a full 60 s / 5 fps survey — the original draws nothing at all. port at pixelIndex=-1: a single red (255,0,0) pixel SCANS the strip left to right and wraps — lit index 0 at t=0, 1 at 0.05, 2 at 0.10, 3 at 0.15, 4 at 0.20, 5 at 0.25, 10 at 0.5, 19 at 1.0, 37 at 2.0, 55 at 3.0, then wrapped to 32 at 5.0 and 25 at 7.9. The port's 60 s survey waterfall shows ~18 clean diagonal traces = a full sweep every ~3.3 s.

The port's auto-scan triggers on ANY negative value, not just -1: -0.5, -1, -5 and -100 all produce the identical scan (portPos 0/19/37/55 at t = 0/1/2/3 s). Positive out-of-range values (60, 100) do NOT trigger it — the port goes black there, same as the original.

The port's auto-scan is TIME-based, not frame-coupled: at 10 / 20 / 40 fps the lit index at t = 1, 2, 3 s is (20,38,56) / (19,37,55) / (18,37,55) — the same position per second to within one pixel across a 4x rate change.

The port's auto-scan rate is a STRIP FRACTION, not an absolute pixel rate: one full sweep in ~3.3 s regardless of rig size — 12 px (index 0→3→7→11 at t = 0/1/2/3 s), 60 px (0→19→37→55), 300 px (4→96→187→279). The original is black in all three.

UNDRIVEN STATE, now measured directly with the new --no-vars flag (meta.json warnings carried '--no-vars: fixups.json var pins NOT applied (orig: pixel; port: pixelIndex)' and sides.orig.varsApplied / sides.port.varsApplied were both {} while varsExported still read ["pixel"] / ["pixelIndex"]). The ORIGINAL is completely inert when nothing writes its var: over 240 s at 5 fps (1200 captured frames) meanBrightness, meanR, meanG, meanB, motion and motionLit are ALL max 0, zeroMotionFrames 1200/1200, brightnessTrend 'steady'; zero lit pixels at t = 0, 0.05, 0.1, 0.25, 0.5, 1, 2, 3, 5, 7.9 s and still zero in a late window at t = 300, 310, 319.9 s. There is no delayed onset and no self-demo. So the port's scan is an INVENTION, not a reproduction of the original's power-on behaviour — the earlier negative-index proxy was exactly right.

The port undriven behaves identically to the port at a negative index — same scan, same phase: lit index 0, 1, 2, 5, 10, 19, 37, 55, 32, 25 at t = 0, 0.05, 0.1, 0.25, 0.5, 1, 2, 3, 5, 7.9 s, matching am-neg-fine pixel-for-pixel. It never settles: still scanning at t = 300/310/319.9 s (index 35/38/39), motionLit avg 84.9 over the 240 s survey, zeroMotionFrames only 14/160 on the 8 s run.

One-sided --no-vars runs isolate the invention cleanly. With --no-vars --vars-orig "pixel=30" (orig driven, port not): orig holds a static red pixel at index 30 while the port scans past it (index 0 at t=0, 37 at t=2, 12 at t=3.9 after wrapping). With --no-vars --vars-port "pixelIndex=30" (port driven, orig not): the port holds a static red pixel at 30 for the whole window while the ORIGINAL stays entirely black. Each side's idle state is therefore a property of that side alone, not an interaction.
feedback: Rename the port's exported variable from 'pixelIndex' to 'pixel' to match the original's varsExported. This pattern's whole purpose is to be driven over the vars API by a mapper/companion client, so the name IS the interface: a client that writes 'pixel' currently drives the original and silently fails to drive the port. This is the single highest-value fix and it costs nothing visually — every driven render already matches byte-for-byte.

Remove the port's idle self-scan. This is now confirmed rather than inferred: with --no-vars the original is black for 240 s straight (all channels max 0, 1200/1200 zero-motion frames, still black at t=320 s), while the port sweeps one red pixel across the whole strip once every ~3.3 s forever. The scan is an invention, not a reproduction of the original's power-on state, and it is what a user actually sees whenever no mapper client is attached. The same scan also fires for any negative index. The port should draw nothing until its var is written to a valid in-range index.

Everything else is already exact and needs no work: single pure-red (255,0,0) pixel, strict integer-equality index match (both sides go black on 29.7 / 30.5 and on any index >= pixelCount), no rounding, no neighbour bleed, no animation, correct flat-index addressing on strip, 32x8 grid and 5x5x5 cloud rigs, and no index ceiling up to at least 299 on a 300-px strip. Do not 'improve' any of these while fixing the two items above.

For a re-judge after the fix, three decisive checks: (a) meta.json sides.*.varsExported reads ["pixel"] on both sides; (b) a --no-vars run where BOTH sides post meanBrightness/motion max 0 and zero lit pixels over a long window (the original's reference behaviour is 1200/1200 zero-motion frames at 240 s / 5 fps); (c) a --vars-orig "pixel=-1" --vars-port "pixel=-1" run where both sides are likewise fully black. The driven paths need no re-verification beyond a spot check — they were byte-identical everywhere tested.
